speaker: April Dunford
title: How to nail your product positioning | April Dunford (Obviously Awesome)
question: How should a very early-stage B2B software startup with few customers approach product positioning differently from a growth-stage company?
guest: I get a lot of calls from super early-stage companies that aren't ready to over-tighten their positioning yet. If you're about to launch or only have a handful of customers, what you really have is a positioning thesis. It's good to go through the exercise and document that thesis internally—who we think we compete with, our differentiated value, who will care most, and our market—so the team is aligned. But if you don't have real customer data yet, in my experience a hundred percent of the time that thesis is partially wrong. It's based on assumptions from customer discovery, not real market proof. So in the early days, it's better to keep your external positioning a bit loose and let the market pull you in a direction you didn't expect. Think of it like designing a fishing net: internally your thesis might be that it's the world's best tuna net. If you launch saying "only for tuna" and you're wrong, you fail hard. If you launch saying it's a net for big fish, fishermen try it, and you might discover it's amazing for grouper. Once you see a real pattern in who loves your product and why, then you tighten up and run at that market.

points.core: Early-stage positioning is an unvalidated thesis that is almost always partially wrong.
points.note: Accept: pre-traction positioning rests on discovery assumptions rather than real buying data, so initial guesses rarely turn out completely accurate. Do not credit: generic advice to iterate or talk to customers.

points.core: Locking external positioning too narrowly early blocks unexpected adjacent market pull.
points.note: Accept: over-tightening external messaging causes hard failure if the initial target is wrong and prevents discovering stronger demand from an unanticipated segment. Do not credit: generic warnings not to alienate potential customers.

points.core: Startups should keep external positioning loose until repeatable customer patterns emerge.
points.note: Accept: document a clear positioning thesis internally for alignment, but keep external framing broader until real adoption signal reveals who loves the product and why before tightening. Do not credit: telling startups to ignore positioning completely.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
An early-stage startup should treat positioning as a hypothesis to test, while a growth-stage company treats it as a known asset to sharpen and scale.

With only a handful of customers, you lack the data to know who values your product most and why. April Dunford, whose framework is widely used here, advises keeping positioning deliberately loose at this stage: cast the net a bit wider, sell to varied prospects, and watch for patterns in who buys fastest, loves the product most, and what they would use instead. Committing too tightly too soon risks optimising for the wrong segment.

In practice that means choosing a narrow best-guess beachhead, stating the problem and the alternative you replace in plain language, and revising often based on founder-led sales conversations. Your evidence is qualitative, and changing course is cheap.

A growth-stage company has enough won and lost deals to identify its best-fit customers with confidence. Its job is to tighten positioning around that segment, pick or define a market category, differentiate against named competitors, and embed the message consistently across sales, marketing, and product. Changes are costlier, so they should be deliberate and triggered by market shifts.

The response warns about optimizing for the wrong segment but does not explain how narrow external messaging can prevent stronger demand from an unexpected segment from surfacing.
The response recommends broad outreach while gathering evidence about who buys and values the product, then tightening around the best-fit segment once deal patterns support it.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
While a growth-stage company anchors its positioning in proven data across hundreds of customers to align large teams and capture broader markets, a very early-stage B2B startup must treat positioning as a fluid, testable hypothesis rather than a fixed identity. With few customers, you lack the pattern recognition required to lock down messaging, so your goal is rapid discovery rather than scalable brand consistency.

Instead of inventing a new category or pitching broad, executive-level transformation like a growth-stage peer, anchor your product in an existing category or position it directly against the manual status quo—such as spreadsheets or stitched-together workflows—so prospects immediately grasp what you replace. Focus narrowly on one acute, urgent pain point for a specific beachhead buyer rather than promising a comprehensive platform, while avoiding over-optimizing for a niche before validating willingness to pay. Keep your positioning deliberately provisional: test your thesis live in founder-led sales calls, listen for the exact words buyers use when the value clicks, and iterate every few conversations until a repeatable pattern of high-conviction customers emerges.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
An early-stage B2B startup should treat positioning as a hypothesis to test, not a story to broadcast. With only a handful of customers, you don't yet know which segment values you most, so position narrowly and on purpose. Pick one specific buyer with one urgent, painful problem. Then learn from real sales conversations which alternatives they compare you to (often spreadsheets, an agency, or doing nothing) and which of your differentiators actually close deals. April Dunford's framework is useful here: start from competitive alternatives, then unique capabilities, then the value those deliver, then the best-fit customers, and only then the market category. Expect to rewrite the positioning often, and favor concrete, problem-focused language over category-creation ambitions.

A growth-stage company has the opposite problem. It has enough data from wins, losses, and retention to know where it fits best, so the job is to codify and scale that positioning. That means consistent messaging across marketing, sales, and product, deliberate expansion into adjacent segments, defending against competitors, and sometimes claiming or shaping a category. Early on, positioning is mostly discovery. Later, it's mostly about staying consistent while you expand.

points.why: The candidate ties limited customer evidence to uncertainty about the best-fit segment and treats revision of the initial thesis as expected.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
A very early-stage B2B startup should treat positioning as a flexible, testable hypothesis rather than a fixed market narrative. Without a large customer base or reliable pattern of wins, founders cannot rely on aggregate data to define their best-fit segment; instead, they should start with a deliberately narrow beachhead, targeting a specific buyer with an acute, urgent pain, and anchor the product against the status quo or manual workarounds prospects actually use today. Because early positioning is primarily a learning tool, it should be tested rapidly in founder-led sales conversations and refined as real buying triggers, objections, and unexpected use cases emerge.

By contrast, a growth-stage company positions from evidence rather than assumptions. With repeatable wins, retention data, and clear customer patterns, it can codify a durable narrative around proven differentiated value, align sales, marketing, and product around a standardized pitch, and expand from an initial wedge into broader use cases, upmarket segments, or an established category.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
With only a few customers, treat positioning as a working hypothesis. Pick a narrow group of buyers with an urgent problem and explain why your product is a better fit than what they do today, even if that’s a spreadsheet or a manual process. Test that story in founder-led sales and onboarding. Pay attention to who buys, what prompted them to act, and what value they actually get. Use those signals to revise your positioning as patterns emerge.

At the growth stage, use evidence across customers and deals to decide which segments and use cases to prioritize. Back up your claims with customer outcomes and make the core story consistent across marketing, sales, and onboarding. Adapt the examples and proof to each buyer, and use win–loss and retention data to decide when the positioning itself needs to change.

points.why: Calling early positioning a working hypothesis conveys uncertainty but does not explain that assumptions made before meaningful buying data are usually partly wrong.
The response recommends targeting a narrow buyer group without explaining how narrow external messaging can hide stronger demand from an unexpected segment.
The response recommends revising positioning as customer patterns emerge but does not commit to keeping external messaging broad until those patterns are clear.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
An early-stage B2B startup should treat positioning as a hypothesis. Start with a narrow answer to three questions: who has the most urgent problem, what do they use today, and why would they switch? Use the few customers you have to learn what triggered their search and how they describe the value. Then test that language in sales conversations with similar prospects. With a small sample, one enthusiastic buyer is a lead to investigate, not enough evidence to reposition the company.

A growth-stage company can use patterns across wins, losses, renewals, and expansion to identify where its advantage holds. Its priority is to make that positioning consistent across sales, marketing, and product, while adapting the examples and proof to each segment. It should revisit the core message when buyer behavior or competition changes.
